title: Oracle DBA
topic: Oracle DBA — architecture, recovery, and production operations: understanding Oracle internals, administering production environments, diagnosing problems, protecting data, and making changes safely. For readers who already know SQL and basic transactions; SQL fundamentals and long installation walkthroughs are out of scope.

concepts.title: Oracle Architecture — Follow a Query and a Commit
concepts.unit: Part I — Understand the Running Database
concepts.brief: Database versus instance; sessions, server processes, background processes; SGA and PGA; buffer cache, shared pool, library cache; datafiles, control files, online redo logs; parse/execute/fetch; the lifecycle of an update and a commit; checkpoints and instance recovery. Central question: what happens between an application issuing SQL and Oracle persisting the result? Include a lab: trace a transaction through Oracle's memory structures, processes, and files.

concepts.title: Transactions, Undo, Redo, and Concurrency
concepts.unit: Part I — Understand the Running Database
concepts.brief: SCNs; undo versus redo; read consistency and multiversioning; statement-level vs transaction-level consistency; row locking and blocking sessions; deadlocks and transaction design; long-running queries and undo retention; diagnosing ORA-01555. Central question: how do readers, writers, consistency, and recovery interact? Lab: create a blocking scenario, identify the blocking session, investigate undo behavior.

concepts.title: Multitenant Architecture — CDBs and PDBs
concepts.unit: Part I — Understand the Running Database
concepts.brief: Container databases and pluggable databases; root, seed, application PDBs; container context for admin commands; common vs local users; services and PDB connections; creating, cloning, opening, closing PDBs; unplug/plug; multitenant implications for security, storage, monitoring, recovery. Central question: are you administering an instance, a CDB, or a PDB? Lab: create and clone a PDB, configure its service, verify administrative scope.

concepts.title: Provisioning, Configuration, and Database Lifecycle
concepts.unit: Part II — Build and Administer the Environment
concepts.brief: Oracle homes and environment configuration; OS users, permissions, limits; database creation with DBCA and scripts; initialization parameters; PFILE and SPFILE; startup/shutdown states; runtime vs persistent configuration changes; baseline configuration and drift; reproducible dev/lab environments. Central question: how do you build an environment another DBA can reproduce and operate? Lab: provision a database and document its configuration baseline.

concepts.title: Connectivity and Oracle Net
concepts.unit: Part II — Build and Administer the Environment
concepts.brief: Listeners, services, connection descriptors; service names vs SIDs; client naming and connection configuration; dedicated vs shared server; authentication and encrypted connections; connection pools from the database perspective; a systematic approach to connection failures. Central question: is the failure in the client, network, listener, service, authentication, or database? Lab: diagnose a connection that works locally but fails from an application host.

concepts.title: Storage, Tablespaces, and Space Management
concepts.unit: Part II — Build and Administer the Environment
concepts.brief: Blocks, extents, segments, tablespaces, datafiles; SYSTEM and SYSAUX; temporary and undo tablespaces; smallfile vs bigfile; autoextend and storage exhaustion; temp-space consumption; segment growth and space reclamation; filesystem vs ASM; capacity planning. Central question: where does space go, and which layer is running out? Lab: investigate a space-related incident and compare remediation options.

concepts.title: Users, Privileges, and Security
concepts.unit: Part II — Build and Administer the Environment
concepts.brief: Users, schemas, roles, profiles; system vs object privileges; administrative privileges and separation of duties; least-privilege service accounts; authentication and password policies; auditing and investigation; encryption and key management concepts; credential handling in scripts; security scope across CDBs and PDBs. Central question: how do you provide necessary access without granting uncontrolled access? Lab: design application and administrative accounts, verify effective privileges.

concepts.title: Backup Engineering with RMAN
concepts.unit: Part III — Protect Data and Recover from Failure
concepts.brief: Recovery objectives and acceptable data loss; ARCHIVELOG mode and archived redo; RMAN; full and incremental backups; backup sets vs image copies; control file and SPFILE protection; retention and deletion policies; backup destinations and failure isolation; backup validation and restore testing; scheduling and monitoring. Central question: which failures can your backup strategy recover from, and how do you know? Lab: implement a backup strategy and prove it with a restore test.

concepts.title: Recovery, Flashback, and Failure Scenarios
concepts.unit: Part III — Protect Data and Recover from Failure
concepts.brief: Instance crashes; lost or damaged datafiles; lost control files; accidental deletion and destructive application changes; point-in-time recovery; recovery into a separate environment; PDB-specific recovery; corruption investigation; choosing between restore/recovery and Flashback; recovery decision trees and validation. Central question: what state must be restored, and which recovery path preserves the most useful data? Lab: recover from deliberately introduced failures and document each decision.

concepts.title: Observability and Troubleshooting
concepts.unit: Part IV — Observe, Diagnose, and Improve
concepts.brief: Data dictionary and V$ views; alert log and diagnostic files; sessions, processes, active SQL, wait events; blocking chains and long-running operations; CPU, memory, I/O, storage-pressure symptoms; baselines, alerts, trend analysis; evidence collection before configuration changes; incident timelines and support packages. Central question: what is the database doing, and what evidence explains the symptom? Lab: investigate a 'database is slow' incident and produce an evidence-based diagnosis.

concepts.title: Performance Diagnosis and SQL Execution
concepts.unit: Part IV — Observe, Diagnose, and Improve
concepts.brief: Actual vs estimated execution plans; cardinality estimates and optimizer statistics; access paths and join methods; bind variables and cursor sharing; hard parsing; index choices and write-side costs; memory pressure and temp usage; SQL trace and TKPROF; AWR, ASH, advisors; edition/licensing checks for diagnostic features; measuring improvements without misleading benchmarks. Central question: what consumes the time, and which change addresses the cause? Lab: diagnose a slow statement, apply a targeted change, measure the result.

concepts.title: Workload Management and Automation
concepts.unit: Part IV — Observe, Diagnose, and Improve
concepts.brief: Resource management and competing workloads; DBMS_SCHEDULER; maintenance windows; repeatable administrative scripts; error handling, logging, exit statuses; idempotent admin tasks; secure credential handling; prechecks, postchecks, approval gates; safe boundaries for automation. Central question: how do you make routine administration predictable and auditable? Lab: build an administrative job with validation, logging, failure reporting, and safe rerun behavior.

concepts.title: Data Movement, Patching, Upgrades, and Migration
concepts.brief: Data Pump export/import; physical copying and cloning; moving schemas and databases between environments; compatibility and dependency checks; Oracle home and patch-management strategy; upgrade planning and rehearsals; data/configuration/application validation; rollback plans; cutover runbooks. Central question: how do you change the environment without losing control of the outcome? Lab: rehearse a migration or upgrade with prechecks, validation, and a rollback plan.

concepts.title: High Availability and Disaster Recovery
concepts.brief: Availability requirements and failure domains; Data Guard architecture; redo transport and apply; standby monitoring and lag; switchover vs failover; DR drills; RAC architecture and shared-storage dependencies; application connection behavior during failures; availability vs recoverability. Central question: which failures does the design tolerate, and what does the application experience? Lab: rehearse a role transition or DR scenario and validate application recovery.

summary: Oracle internals, production operations, backup and recovery, diagnosis, and safe change — a plain-words operations book for DBAs, with labs, runbooks, and a running order-processing case study on Oracle Database 19c.
